items.title: Existing Home Sales Treading Same Old Water
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content: <article>If you're busy, we can make this quick. Existing home sales dropped sharply from over 6m units per year starting in 2022 and had bottomed out around 4m units per year by the end of 2023. They've done essentially nothing exciting since then and the latest update is no exception. The end.     If you prefer to read an article-sized article, here you go:  Existing-home sales edged higher in September with The National Association of REALTORS® reporting a  1.5% increase  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  3.99 million . August and September mark the two slowest months for home sales this year, as higher borrowing costs continued to limit the pool of qualified buyers.  “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” Yun said. Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed rate climbed to  6.86% in September , up from 6.67% in August and 6.35% a year earlier.  Inventory continued to offer buyers more options than they had a year ago, although the latest increase was relatively modest. Total housing inventory reached  1.60 million units , up  1.9% from August  and  4.6% year over year .  Buyers may also have more room to negotiate as homes take longer to sell. The median time on market increased to  33 days , up from 31 days in August. Yun said the combination of higher inventory and longer selling times could require sellers to offer price reductions or other incentives to attract buyers.</article>

items.title: Only a Modest Decline For Mortgage Apps. Next Week Should Improve
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>Mortgage applications continued to lose ground as mortgage rates held near their highest levels in nearly three years. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  2.7% decline  in total mortgage application volume for the week ending October 9.  That's an important date, because a substantial majority of a fairly sharp decline in interest rates occurred AFTER October 9. As such, next week's data is a great opportunity to see the impact of lower rates.   Purchase activity took another step back, with the seasonally adjusted Purchase Index falling  4%  for the week and running  16% below year-ago levels . Refinances were nearly unchanged, slipping just 0.4%, but remained  56% lower  than a year earlier.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate edged up to  7.50% , its highest level since November 2023 and more than a percentage point above its level a year ago. MBA's Joel Kan notes,  “As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM loans to help lower their monthly payments."   ARMs accounted for  10.5% of all applications , the highest share since October 2025. The refinance share also ticked higher, reaching 37.7% of total applications from 37.0% the previous week, with a 5% drop in FHA refinance applications being the main driver of the small overall decline.  Mortgage Rate Summary:  
  30yr Fixed:  7.50% (from 7.49%) |  Points:  0.83 (from 0.84) 
  15yr Fixed:  6.87% (from 6.71%) |  Points:  0.90 (from 1.05) 
  Jumbo 30yr:  7.49% (from 7.39%) |  Points:  0.70 (from 0.52) 
  FHA:  7.19% (from 7.14%) |  Points:  1.21 (from 1.36) 
  5/1 ARM:  6.54% (from 6.43%) |  Points:  1.13 (from 1.69)</article>

items.title: Higher Rates Sapped Mortgage Demand, Surprising No One
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>Mortgage demand shocked no one by declining last week as mortgage rates climbed to their highest level in nearly three years. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  6% drop  in total mortgage application volume for the week ending September 25.  Both sides of the market moved lower, with the seasonally adjusted Purchase Index falling  4%  and refinance applications dropping  9% . MBA said purchase and refinance activity both reached their  slowest weekly pace since 2025 .    Refinances always get hit hardest by rate spikes with the index now  56% lower  than a year earlier. Government refinance applications fell 13% from the prior week.    "Mortgage rates jumped to their highest level in almost three years, pushing borrowers to the sidelines," said Joel Kan, MBA's Vice President and Deputy Chief Economist. He noted that the 30-year fixed rate reached 7.30%, its highest level since November 2023.  There was another sign that some borrowers are looking for alternatives to the traditional fixed-rate mortgage. ARM loans accounted for  10.3%  of all applications, the highest share since October 2025. Kan said ARM rates were roughly 80 basis points below fixed rates, although the average 5/1 ARM rate also moved higher in the latest survey.  Mortgage Rate Summary:  
  30yr Fixed:  7.30% (from 7.12%) |  Points:  0.75 (from 0.73) 
  15yr Fixed:  6.56% (from 6.43%) |  Points:  1.02 (from 1.15) 
  Jumbo 30yr:  7.27% (from 7.15%) |  Points:  0.50 (from 0.53) 
  FHA:  6.97% (from 6.78%) |  Points:  1.18 (from 0.96) 
  5/1 ARM:  6.47% (from 6.10%) |  Points:  1.20 (from 0.76)</article>

items.title: Home Prices Keep Climbing, Just Not Everywhere
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content: <article>Home prices picked up a little more speed in July, as both  FHFA  and the S&P Cotality  Case-Shiller  Home Price Indices showed stronger annual appreciation than in their previous readings. The gains remain relatively modest by historical standards, and while nominal prices are still moving higher nationally, the picture looks considerably less impressive after accounting for inflation.  The FHFA House Price Index rose  0.3%  from June to July, bringing the annual increase to  2.6% . While the national market is still technically appreciating, there's more and more variation between different metro areas with some holding steady or even contracting.  Case-Shiller tells a similar story, though its national measure is running at a somewhat slower pace. The  U.S. National Home Price Index  rose  1.9%  year over year in July, up from 1.6% in June. The 10-City Composite increased  3.4% , while the 20-City Composite was up  2.5% .    The annual price appreciation chart shows a nice little uptick, but the takeaway is tempered in inflation-adjusted terms. Both of the big U.S. inflation reports showed annual changes of 3.4% last month, and even higher in July (the month that lines up with these home price reports). Any way you slice it, that means home prices aren't keeping pace with broader inflation. Whether or not that's a bad thing is another story. Some would say it wouldn't be the end of the world for prices to merely hold steady and allow income growth to slowly chip away at affordability. </article>
